claim: Dysfunction of the basal ganglia produces severe deficits in the timing, initiation, and vigor of movement.
source: Dysfunction of the basal ganglia produces severe deficits in the timing, initiation, and vigor of movement.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work on timing (Buhusi and Meck, 2005), vigor (Turner and Desmurget, 2010), and initiation (Mink, 1996) deficits.

claim: Feedback via axon collaterals of substantia nigra projection neurons control the gain of the basal ganglia output.
source: In this study, we show that feedback via axon collaterals of substantia nigra projection neurons control the gain of the basal ganglia output.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in multiple figures (e.g., Figure 3).

claim: The substantia nigra pars reticulata is the primary source of output from the sensorimotor basal ganglia in rodents.
source: The substantia nigra (SN) pars reticulata (SNr) is the primary source of output from the sensorimotor basal ganglia in rodents (Gerfen, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gerfen, 2004.

claim: The vast majority of neurons in the SNr are projection neurons that synthesize and release GABA.
source: The vast majority of neurons in the SNr are projection neurons that synthesize and release the neurotransmitter ϒ-aminobutryic acid (GABA).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SNr neuron types.

claim: Nigral projection neurons elaborate axon collaterals within the SN.
source: In addition to these long range targets, nigral projection neurons also elaborate axon collaterals within the SN (Mailly et al., 2003; Cebrián et al., 2005; Deniau et al., 2007a).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple anatomical studies cited.

claim: There are no known interneurons in the SNr.
source: There are no known interneurons in the SNr (Deniau et al., 2007a), and thus collaterals of projection neurons are the sole source of intrinsic feedback for the basal ganglia output.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Deniau et al., 2007a.

claim: Collaterals of projection neurons are the sole source of intrinsic feedback for the basal ganglia output.
source: There are no known interneurons in the SNr (Deniau et al., 2007a), and thus collaterals of projection neurons are the sole source of intrinsic feedback for the basal ganglia output.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the absence of interneurons combined with anatomical knowledge.

claim: Anatomical reconstructions have indicated that the axon collaterals of SNr projection neurons are sparse.
source: Anatomical reconstructions have indicated that the axon collaterals of SNr projection neurons are sparse (Mailly et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mailly et al., 2003.

claim: A salient or conditioned stimulus can lead to phasic changes in the activity of SNr neurons in rodents.
source: Recent work has shown that a salient or conditioned stimulus (CS), for example an auditory tone, can lead to phasic changes in the activity of SNr neurons in rodents (Schmidt et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Schmidt et al., 2013.

claim: Short-latency modulations of SNr activity are predictive of the initiation of conditioned behavioral responses.
source: Moreover, these short-latency modulations of activity are predictive of the initiation of conditioned behavioral responses—that is action selection (Pan et al., 2013; Schmidt et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pan et al., 2013 and Schmidt et al., 2013.

claim: The level of activation of the SNr population prior to a stimulus is inversely correlated with the modulation of the response of an individual neuron to that stimulus.
source: We found that both the population (−0.1; p<0.001 permutation test) and 22/32 individual sessions exhibited significant negative correlations (−0.12 ± 0.05 SD; p<0.05, permutation test; Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of in vivo recording data presented in Figure 1.

claim: ChR2 was selectively expressed in SNr GABA neurons via viral injection in Gad2-cre mice.
source: In one set of experiments an adeno-associated virus (AAV) that expressed a cre-dependent ChR2 transgene (Atasoy et al., 2008) was injected into the SNr of a mouse line in which cre-recombinase was expressed under the glutamic acid decarboxylase (Gad2) promoter to target expression to SNr GABA neurons (hereafter referred to as Gad2-ChR2; Figure 2A,C).
evidence: This is a methodological claim supported by the experimental design and Figure 2.

claim: ChR2 is robustly expressed in SNr GABA neurons in the Thy1-ChR2 transgenic mouse line.
source: In the other, we exploited a transgenic mouse line which has strong expression of ChR2 under the control of the thymus cell antigen 1 (Thy1) promoter (Arenkiel et al., 2007), (hereafter referred to as Thy1-ChR2; Figure 2B,D). In this transgenic line ChR2 is robustly expressed in SNr GABA neurons, but not in SN dopaminergic neurons (Pan et al., 2013;) or in upstream projection neurons of the dorsal striatum (data available from the authors on request).
evidence: This is a methodological claim supported by the experimental design, Figure 2, and citation to Pan et al., 2013.

claim: ChR2 is not expressed in SN dopaminergic neurons in the Thy1-ChR2 mouse line.
source: In this transgenic line ChR2 is robustly expressed in SNr GABA neurons, but not in SN dopaminergic neurons (Pan et al., 2013;) or in upstream projection neurons of the dorsal striatum (data available from the authors on request).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pan et al., 2013 and unpublished data.

claim: Wide-field illumination reliably evoked action potentials in SNr GABA neurons in Gad2-ChR2 mice.
source: In vitro wide-field illumination of midbrain slice (0.5 ms light pulse, 10 Hz, cyan arrows) reliably evoked action potentials in SNr GABA neurons in Gad2-ChR2 (C; n = 12/20 cells) and Thy1-ChR2 (D; n = 21/21 cells) mice
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Wide-field illumination reliably evoked action potentials in SNr GABA neurons in Thy1-ChR2 mice.
source: In vitro wide-field illumination of midbrain slice (0.5 ms light pulse, 10 Hz, cyan arrows) reliably evoked action potentials in SNr GABA neurons in Gad2-ChR2 (C; n = 12/20 cells) and Thy1-ChR2 (D; n = 21/21 cells) mice
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Local inhibition was sufficient to suppress direct light-evoked spiking in SNr projection neurons under control conditions.
source: Direct light-evoked spiking in the recorded neuron was substantially, or in some cases completely, suppressed under control conditions (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: Reliable light-evoked spiking was present following application of gabazine to block local inhibition.
source: However, reliable light-evoked spiking was always present following application of the GABAA receptor antagonist gabazine (Gbz) to block local inhibition (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The response of the SNr population showed a significant increase as a function of stimulus duration.
source: We found that the response of the population showed a significant increase as a function of stimulus duration and the magnitude of the increase was significantly reduced by the presence of feedback inhibition (two-factor ANOVA; p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The magnitude of the response increase was significantly reduced by the presence of feedback inhibition.
source: We found that the response of the population showed a significant increase as a function of stimulus duration and the magnitude of the increase was significantly reduced by the presence of feedback inhibition (two-factor ANOVA; p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Baseline firing was unaffected by removal of inhibition.
source: Consistent with a divisive gain control, we found that baseline firing was unaffected by removal of inhibition (Figure 3G, open circles).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Suppression of spiking was characterized by a significant decrease in the duration of the evoked spiking.
source: Consistent with this prediction we found that suppression of spiking was characterized by a significant decrease in the duration of the evoked spiking (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: There was a significant correlation in the extent of feedback inhibition in paired recordings.
source: Consistent with this prediction, we found that there was a significant correlation (Pearson's correlation, p<0.01 permutation test) in paired recordings (Figure 3I).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Unitary release events produced relatively weak mIPSCs (∼150 pS).
source: Moreover, we found that unitary release events produced relatively weak mIPSCs (∼150 pS) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The expected rate of spontaneous IPSCs is approximately 75–300 Hz based on anatomical estimates.
source: Thus, with a relatively low release probability (<0.5), we would predict 75–300 Hz of uIPSCs.
evidence: This is a calculation based on equation (1) and anatomical estimates.

claim: The predicted rate of uIPSCs corresponds well to the rate estimated directly from voltage clamp recordings.
source: This corresponds well to the rate of uIPSCs estimated directly from voltage clamp recordings (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A–C.

claim: Repetitive stimulation of SNr collaterals fails to completely depress transmission.
source: Consistent with this estimate, we also show that repetitive stimulation of SNr collaterals fails to completely depress transmission (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) consistent with a vesicular release probability low enough to allow vesicle recycling to keep pace with release.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Pharmacological blockade of inhibition has no significant effect on the tonic firing of SNr projection neurons.
source: These observations suggest that there is indeed a substantial background rate of IPSCs that, when pharmacologically blocked, has no significant effect on the tonic firing of SNr projection neurons (Atherton and Bevan, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Atherton and Bevan, 2005 and experimental data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The sensitivity of the spike rate to increasing inhibition was much reduced compared to the sensitivity to increasing excitation.
source: Indeed, we found that the sensitivity of the spike rate to increasing inhibition was much reduced compared to the sensitivity to increasing excitation.
evidence: This claim is supported by dynamic clamp experimental data shown in Figure 4D–F.

claim: Collateral inhibition resulted in a strong suppression of evoked spiking and was sufficient to truncate evoked responses.
source: Collateral inhibition resulted in a strong suppression of evoked spiking and was sufficient to truncate evoked responses, often after only a few milliseconds.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Evoked IPSCs from feedback nigral collaterals exhibited rapid kinetics characterized by short, monosynaptic latencies (1.93 ± 0.02 ms).
source: Evoked IPSCs from feedback nigral collaterals recorded in Gad2-ChR2 mouse exhibited rapid kinetics characterized by short, monosynaptic latencies (Figure 5D; 1.93 ± 0.02 ms), rapid 10–90% rise times (Figure 5E; 0.53 ± 0.01 ms) and rapid decay time constants (τ) (Figure 5F; 5.64 ± 0.14 ms).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Evoked IPSCs from feedback nigral collaterals exhibited rapid 10–90% rise times (0.53 ± 0.01 ms).
source: Evoked IPSCs from feedback nigral collaterals recorded in Gad2-ChR2 mouse exhibited rapid kinetics characterized by short, monosynaptic latencies (Figure 5D; 1.93 ± 0.02 ms), rapid 10–90% rise times (Figure 5E; 0.53 ± 0.01 ms) and rapid decay time constants (τ) (Figure 5F; 5.64 ± 0.14 ms).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Evoked IPSCs from feedback nigral collaterals exhibited rapid decay time constants (5.64 ± 0.14 ms).
source: Evoked IPSCs from feedback nigral collaterals recorded in Gad2-ChR2 mouse exhibited rapid kinetics characterized by short, monosynaptic latencies (Figure 5D; 1.93 ± 0.02 ms), rapid 10–90% rise times (Figure 5E; 0.53 ± 0.01 ms) and rapid decay time constants (τ) (Figure 5F; 5.64 ± 0.14 ms).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Striatonigral IPSCs had significantly longer latencies (2.51 ± 0.02 ms) compared to intranigral inhibitory synapses.
source: In contrast to the intranigral inhibitory synapses, we found that striatonigral IPSCs recorded in Drd1a-ChR2 mouse had significantly longer latencies (Figure 5D; 2.51 ± 0.02 ms p<0.001), slower 10–90% rise times (Figure 5E; 0.75 ± 0.014 ms, p<0.001) and slower decay τ (Figure 5F; 9.00 ± 0.14 ms, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Striatonigral IPSCs had slower 10–90% rise times (0.75 ± 0.014 ms) compared to intranigral inhibitory synapses.
source: In contrast to the intranigral inhibitory synapses, we found that striatonigral IPSCs recorded in Drd1a-ChR2 mouse had significantly longer latencies (Figure 5D; 2.51 ± 0.02 ms p<0.001), slower 10–90% rise times (Figure 5E; 0.75 ± 0.014 ms, p<0.001) and slower decay τ (Figure 5F; 9.00 ± 0.14 ms, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Striatonigral IPSCs had slower decay τ (9.00 ± 0.14 ms) compared to intranigral inhibitory synapses.
source: In contrast to the intranigral inhibitory synapses, we found that striatonigral IPSCs recorded in Drd1a-ChR2 mouse had significantly longer latencies (Figure 5D; 2.51 ± 0.02 ms p<0.001), slower 10–90% rise times (Figure 5E; 0.75 ± 0.014 ms, p<0.001) and slower decay τ (Figure 5F; 9.00 ± 0.14 ms, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: With saturating stimulation, intranigral synapses contributed as large or greater inhibition than the direct pathway.
source: Perhaps most surprisingly, we observed that with saturating stimulation, intranigral synapses contributed as large or greater inhibition than the major afferent source of inhibitory input, the direct pathway (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Collateral synapses within the SNr exhibited paired pulse ratios less than 1 (PPR = 0.91 ± 0.03).
source: We found that collateral synapses within the SNr exhibited paired pulse ratios (PPR) less than 1 (Figure 5H; PPR = 0.91 ± 0.03).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The striatonigral synapse was modestly facilitating (PPR = 1.17 ± 0.05).
source: While, in direct contrast, the striatonigral synapse was modestly facilitating (Figure 5H; PPR = 1.17 ± 0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: There was no correlation between the location of individual neurons and the source of the strongest inhibition within the SNr.
source: In contrast to the first prediction, we found that there was no correlation between the location of individual neurons and the source of the strongest inhibition within the SNr.
evidence: This claim is supported by circuit mapping data shown in Figure 6E–F.

claim: Neurons with non-overlapping dendritic arbors could have largely overlapping inhibitory receptive fields.
source: In other words, we found that neurons with non-overlapping dendritic arbors could have largely overlapping inhibitory receptive fields (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by circuit mapping data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The correlation in the maps obtained from individual neurons was a monotonically decreasing function of distance between neurons.
source: We found that the correlation in the maps obtained from individual neurons was a monotonically decreasing function of distance between neurons (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by circuit mapping data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: There was no clear organization between the striatonigral projection and the maps of feedback inhibition.
source: However, we found no clear organization between the striatonigral projection and the maps of feedback inhibition (Figure 7A,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by circuit mapping data shown in Figure 7A,C.

claim: Projection neurons receive feedback inhibition from a diffuse microcircuit independent of the discontinuous topography of feed forward input.
source: However, the consistent fall off of the correlation in inhibitory response maps across neurons (Figure 7B) suggests that projection neurons receive feedback inhibition from a diffuse microcircuit and independent of the discontinuous topography of feed forward input.
evidence: This claim is supported by circuit mapping data shown in Figure 7B and inference from the data.

claim: Some units exhibited direct excitation by photostimulation followed by suppression.
source: Some units (e.g., s06u01) exhibited direct excitation by photostimulation followed by suppression. While other units (e.g., s03u21) located at a more eccentric position on the array exhibited a delayed (one 5 ms PSTH bin) suppression of firing.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo recording data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Some units exhibited a delayed suppression of firing without direct excitation.
source: While other units (e.g., s03u21) located at a more eccentric position on the array exhibited a delayed (one 5 ms PSTH bin) suppression of firing.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo recording data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Inhibition and excitation were recruited with a similar dependence on stimulus intensity.
source: We found that inhibition and excitation were recruited with a similar dependence on stimulus intensity consistent with a model in which intranigral inhibition produces a divisive gain effect on the output of SNr projection neurons (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo recording data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Functional inhibition can extend for hundreds of microns beyond the focus of excitation in vivo.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that functional inhibition can extend for hundreds of microns beyond the focus of excitation in vivo as was observed in vitro.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo recording data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The only intrinsic source of feedback to the main basal ganglia output nucleus, the SNr, is the microcircuit formed by collaterals of projection neurons.
source: However, the only intrinsic source of feedback to the main basal ganglia output nucleus, the SNr, is the microcircuit formed by collaterals of projection neurons (Deniau et al., 2007b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Deniau et al., 2007b.

claim: The unique properties of the SNr microcircuit combine to implement a potent feedback inhibitory circuit that can exert a divisive gain control effect on the basal ganglia output.
source: Here, we show that the unique properties of the SNr microcircuit—both intrinsic properties of projection neurons and the organization of functional activity—combine to implement a potent feedback inhibitory circuit that can exert a divisive gain control effect on the basal ganglia output.
evidence: This is a summary claim of the main findings supported by multiple experimental results throughout the manuscript.

claim: The SN microcircuit appears to modify transient responses to salient sensory stimuli in a manner consistent with negative feedback.
source: In behaving mice, we observed that the SN microcircuit appears to modify transient responses to salient sensory stimuli, in our case a CS, in a manner consistent with negative feedback (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo recording data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Individual intranigral synapses were weak, but potent inhibition resulted from a spatially diffuse microcircuit in vitro and in vivo.
source: (4) individual intranigral synapses were weak, but potent inhibition resulted from a spatially diffuse microcircuit in vitro (Figures 6 and 7) and in vivo (Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6, 7, and 8.

claim: The functional architecture of the intranigral microcircuit is sufficient to provide robust feedback inhibition that is proportional to the activity SN population.
source: Together, these data indicate that the functional architecture of the intranigral microcircuit is sufficient to provide robust feedback inhibition that is proportional to the activity SN population—that is it provides a potent gain control on the output of the basal ganglia.
evidence: This is a summary claim of the main findings supported by multiple experimental results throughout the manuscript.

claim: The striatonigral and intranigral projections were organized independently.
source: We further confirmed this observation by combining axonal tracing together with circuit mapping to demonstrate that the striatonigral and intranigral projections were organized independently (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by circuit mapping data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The gain control provided by the intranigral microcircuit could reflect a global negative feedback signal that spans individual channels of feed forward basal ganglia activity.
source: Thus, our data imply that the gain control provided by the intranigral microcircuit could reflect a global negative feedback signal that spans individual channels of feed forward basal ganglia activity.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data on the spatial organization of the intranigral microcircuit.

claim: Both viral-mediated infection and the Thy1-ChR2 transgenic mouse line exhibited cell-type specific expression of ChR2 in GABAergic neurons of the SN, but not in dopamine neurons.
source: Both viral-mediated infection of GABAergic neurons in the SNr and the Thy1-ChR2 transgenic mouse line exhibited cell-type specific expression of ChR2 in GABAergic neurons of the SN, but not in dopamine neurons.
evidence: This is a methodological claim supported by the experimental design and data in Figure 2.

claim: Both approaches had indistinguishable properties of inhibition onto both GABAergic projection neurons and onto dopamine neurons.
source: Importantly, both approaches had indistinguishable properties of inhibition onto both GABAergic projection neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and onto dopamine neurons (Pan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and citation to Pan et al., 2013.

claim: Neurons of the external globus pallidus express ChR2 in the Thy1-ChR2 mouse line.
source: However, in addition to expression in the SNr, we did also observe that neurons of the external globus pallidus (GPe) express ChR2.
evidence: This is an observation from the Thy1-ChR2 mouse line.

claim: Potent feedback inhibition could be observed in Gad2-ChR2 mice.
source: Nonetheless, we found that potent feedback inhibition could be observed in Gad2-ChR2 mice and that stimulation of GPe axons yielded relatively less inhibition in SNr neurons than either the striatonigral or intranigral pathways under our stimulus conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Gad2-ChR2 mice.

claim: Stimulation of GPe axons yielded relatively less inhibition in SNr neurons than either the striatonigral or intranigral pathways.
source: Nonetheless, we found that potent feedback inhibition could be observed in Gad2-ChR2 mice and that stimulation of GPe axons yielded relatively less inhibition in SNr neurons than either the striatonigral or intranigral pathways under our stimulus conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing different inhibitory pathways.

claim: A broad distribution of firing rates combined with relatively weak individual connections could produce inhibition that is essentially tonic and too small to significantly affect intrinsic currents that drive repetitive spiking.
source: One possibility suggested by our data is that a broad distribution of firing rates (Figure 8) combined with relatively weak individual connections (Figure 4) could produce inhibition that is essentially tonic and too small to significantly affect intrinsic currents that drive repetitive spiking (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and so is counteracted via subthreshold inward currents necessary for repetitive firing.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed based on experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 8.

claim: There is a high frequency (200 Hz) of spontaneous IPSCs bombarding SNr projection neurons.
source: We provided support for such a model by demonstrating that there is, indeed, a high frequency (200 Hz) of spontaneous IPSCs bombarding SNr projection neurons (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Simulation of a steady background rate of IPSCs using dynamic clamp revealed a relative insensitivity of spike rate to a tonic net inhibitory background of inputs.
source: Further consistent with this model, simulation of a steady background rate of IPSCs using dynamic clamp revealed a relative insensitivity of spike rate to a tonic net inhibitory background of inputs (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by dynamic clamp experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: This mechanism combining intrinsic properties and synaptic properties is sufficient for a population of spontaneously active inhibitory neurons to implement divisive gain control in the apparent absence of interneurons.
source: This mechanism combining intrinsic properties and synaptic properties is sufficient for a population of spontaneously active inhibitory neurons to implement divisive gain control in the apparent absence of interneurons (Deniau et al., 2007b).
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion based on the experimental data and citation to Deniau et al., 2007b.

claim: This represents a novel circuit mechanism for divisive gain control.
source: To our knowledge this represents a novel circuit mechanism for divisive gain control (Silver, 2010; Figure 9).
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the mechanism, supported by comparison to prior work (Silver, 2010) and illustrated in Figure 9.

claim: The feed forward pathways of the basal ganglia are topographically organized and largely independent.
source: On the one hand, it has been argued for some time that the feed forward pathways of the basal ganglia are topographically organized and largely independent (Mink, 1996; Haber, 2003; Hikosaka, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mink, 1996; Haber, 2003; Hikosaka, 2007.

claim: Movement is thought to occur when a focal population of projection neurons becomes inhibited by feed forward input and thus disinhibits downstream pre-motor structures.
source: Movement is thus thought to occur when a focal population of projection neurons becomes inhibited by feed forward input and thus disinhibits downstream pre-motor structures.
evidence: This is a description of a prevailing model in the field.

claim: During focal activation of the SNr, collateral inhibition may be thought of as a mechanism for contrast enhancement akin to the role of lateral inhibition in sensory systems.
source: Thus, during focal activation of the SNr, collateral inhibition may be thought of as a mechanism for contrast enhancement akin to the role of lateral inhibition in sensory systems.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the function of collateral inhibition.

claim: Time locked, bidirectional changes in the firing of SNr projection neurons are commonly observed prior to and during movement in mice and primates.
source: This mechanism may be reflected in the time locked, bidirectional changes in the firing of SNr projection neurons that are commonly observed prior to and during movement in mice (Pan et al., 2013; Fan et al., 2012) and primates (Turner and Anderson, 1997; Nevet et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pan et al., 2013; Fan et al., 2012; Turner and Anderson, 1997; Nevet et al., 2007.

claim: While the direct striatonigral pathway is topographically organized there is considerable divergence in the corticostriatal input in mice.
source: On the other hand, while the direct striatonigral pathway is topographically organized there is considerable divergence in the corticostriatal input in mice (Pan et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pan et al., 2010.

claim: There may be less precise topographic organization of the indirect pathway that enters the SNr via the subthalamic nucleus.
source: In addition, there may be less precise topographic organization of the indirect pathway that enters the SNr via the subthalamic nucleus (Bolam et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bolam et al., 2000.

claim: The subthalamic nucleus receives direct cortical input and ascending input from the midbrain and hindbrain.
source: The subthalamic nucleus also receives direct cortical input and ascending input from the midbrain (Coizet et al., 2009) and hindbrain (Bevan and Bolam, 1995; Winn, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Coizet et al., 2009; Bevan and Bolam, 1995; Winn, 2006.

claim: Individual neurons that constitute the output of cortical areas project to multiple subcortical structures.
source: While there are mechanisms that could maintain activity within a fixed dynamic range in upstream structures (Silver, 2010), individual neurons that constitute the output of cortical areas project to multiple subcortical structures (Kita and Kita, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Silver, 2010 and Kita and Kita, 2012.

claim: It is unlikely that the dynamic range of even the cortical output is appropriate for the diverse computations performed in all target structures.
source: It is therefore unlikely that the dynamic range of even the cortical output is appropriate for the diverse computations performed in all target structures.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the fact that cortical neurons project to multiple subcortical structures.

claim: Divisive gain control supplied by a diffuse but potent inhibitory microcircuit could be well suited to ensure that activity remains within a fixed dynamic range.
source: Thus, divisive gain control supplied by a diffuse but potent inhibitory microcircuit could be well suited to ensure that activity remains within a fixed dynamic range.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the function of the intranigral microcircuit.

claim: Cortical afferents to the basal ganglia are derived from an estimated 17 million neurons spanning the majority of the roughly 100 mm3 volume of neocortex.
source: Cortical afferents to the basal ganglia are derived from an estimated 17 million neurons (Zheng and Wilson, 2002) spanning the majority of the roughly 100 mm3 volume of neocortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zheng and Wilson, 2002.

claim: Cortical inputs are funneled through the basal ganglia and will ultimately terminate on approximately 30,000 projection neurons within the roughly 4 mm2 volume of the SN.
source: These inputs are funneled through the basal ganglia and will ultimately terminate on approximately 30,000 projection neurons (Oorschot, 1996) within the roughly 4 mm2 volume of the SN.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Oorschot, 1996.

claim: Dendrites of nigral projection neurons and intranigral inhibition that extends over hundreds of microns could shape activity derived from cortical inputs separated by several millimeters.
source: Dendrites of nigral projection neurons and intranigral inhibition that extends over hundreds of microns (Grofova et al., 1982; Mailly et al., 2001) could therefore shape activity derived from cortical inputs separated by several millimeters.
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical data cited (Grofova et al., 1982; Mailly et al., 2001) and the experimental findings.

claim: Existing functional models focus on the feed forward structure of processing within the intrinsic basal ganglia circuitry.
source: Existing functional models focus on the feed forward structure of processing within the intrinsic basal ganglia circuitry (e.g., Albin et al., 1989; DeLong, 2000; Mink, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Albin et al., 1989; DeLong, 2000; Mink, 1996.

claim: The observation that intranigral inhibition is strong relative to the major source of feed forward input suggests that local processing of diverse streams of information in the SN could be critical for generating dynamics in the basal ganglia output.
source: However, our observation that intranigral inhibition is strong relative to the major source of feed forward input suggests that local processing of diverse streams of information in the SN could be critical for generating dynamics in the basal ganglia output.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental findings about the strength of intranigral inhibition.

claim: The diverse impairments characteristic of pathological disruption of basal ganglia function could reflect, in part, a control system operating outside of a stable regime.
source: We hypothesize that the diverse impairments characteristic of pathological disruption of basal ganglia function could reflect, in part, a control system operating outside of a stable regime.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the role of the intranigral microcircuit in disease.

claim: There is evidence of perturbed dynamics in the SNr in disease models.
source: Although there is evidence of perturbed dynamics in the SNr in disease models (Ibanez-Sandoval et al., 2007; Samadi et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2010), the specific contribution of the intranigral microcircuit to the diverse behavioral impairments observed in diseases afflicting the basal ganglia circuit remains unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ibanez-Sandoval et al., 2007; Samadi et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2010.

claim: The specific contribution of the intranigral microcircuit to the diverse behavioral impairments observed in diseases afflicting the basal ganglia circuit remains unclear.
source: Although there is evidence of perturbed dynamics in the SNr in disease models (Ibanez-Sandoval et al., 2007; Samadi et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2010), the specific contribution of the intranigral microcircuit to the diverse behavioral impairments observed in diseases afflicting the basal ganglia circuit remains unclear.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of current knowledge.

claim: Adult transgenic mice (10–30 weeks old) expressing ChR2-YFP fusion gene under the control of the mouse thymus cell antigen 1 promoter were used for in vitro experiments.
